{{Short description|Pattern in mathematics and computer science}}
In [[mathematics]] and [[theoretical computer science]], a pattern is an '''unavoidable pattern''' if it is unavoidable on any finite alphabet.

== Definitions ==

=== Pattern ===
Like a word, a pattern (also called ''term'') is a sequence of symbols over some [[Alphabet (formal languages)|alphabet]].

The minimum multiplicity of the pattern ''<math>p</math>'' is ''<math>m(p)=\min(\mathrm{count_p}(x):x \in p)</math>'' where ''<math>\mathrm{count_p}(x)</math>'' is the number of occurrence of symbol ''<math>x</math>'' in pattern ''<math>p</math>''. In other words, it is the number of occurrences in ''<math>p</math>'' of the least frequently occurring symbol in ''<math>p</math>''. 

=== Instance ===
Given finite alphabets <math>\Sigma</math> and <math>\Delta</math>, a word <math>x\in\Sigma^*</math> is an instance of the pattern <math>p\in\Delta^*</math> if there exists a non-erasing [[semigroup morphism]] <math>f:\Delta^*\rightarrow\Sigma^*</math> such that <math>f(p)=x</math>, where <math>\Sigma^*</math> denotes the [[Kleene star]] of <math>\Sigma</math>. Non-erasing means that <math>f(a)\neq\varepsilon</math> for all <math>a\in\Delta</math>, where <math>\varepsilon</math> denotes the [[empty string]].

=== Avoidance / Matching ===
A word <math>w</math> is said to ''match'', or ''encounter'', a pattern <math>p</math> if a factor (also called ''subword'' or ''[[substring]]'') of <math>w</math> is an instance of <math>p</math>. Otherwise, <math>w</math> is said to avoid <math>p</math>, or to be <math>p</math>-free. This definition can be generalized to the case of an infinite <math>w</math>, based on a generalized definition of "substring".

=== Avoidability / Unavoidability on a specific alphabet ===
A pattern <math>p</math> is ''unavoidable'' on a finite alphabet <math>\Sigma</math> if each sufficiently long word <math>x\in\Sigma^*</math> must match <math>p</math>; formally: if <math>\exists n\in \Nu. \ \forall x\in\Sigma^*. \ (|x|\geq n \implies x \text{ matches } p)</math>. Otherwise, <math>p</math> is ''avoidable'' on <math>\Sigma</math>, which implies there exist infinitely many words over the alphabet <math>\Sigma</math> that avoid <math>p</math>. 

By [[Kőnig's lemma]], pattern <math>p</math> is avoidable on <math>\Sigma</math> [[if, and only if|if and only if]] there exists an [[infinite sequence|infinite word]] <math>w\in \Sigma^\omega</math> that avoids <math>p</math>.<ref name="Lothaire2001" />

=== Maximal ''p''-free word ===
Given a pattern <math>p</math> and an alphabet ''<math>\Sigma</math>''. A <math>p</math>-free word ''<math>w\in\Sigma^*</math>'' is a maximal <math>p</math>-free word over ''<math>\Sigma</math>'' if <math>aw</math> and <math>wa</math> match <math>p</math> <math>\forall a\in\Sigma</math>.

=== Avoidable / Unavoidable pattern ===
A pattern ''<math>p</math>'' is an unavoidable pattern (also called ''blocking term'') if ''<math>p</math>'' is unavoidable on any finite alphabet.

If a pattern is unavoidable and not limited to a specific alphabet, then it is unavoidable for any finite alphabet by default. Conversely, if a pattern is said to be avoidable and not limited to a specific alphabet, then it is avoidable on some finite alphabet by default.

=== ''k''-avoidable / ''k''-unavoidable ===
A pattern ''<math>p</math>'' is ''<math>k</math>''-avoidable if ''<math>p</math>'' is avoidable on an alphabet ''<math>\Sigma</math>'' of size ''<math>k</math>''. Otherwise, ''<math>p</math>'' is ''<math>k</math>''-unavoidable, which means ''<math>p</math>'' is unavoidable on every alphabet of size ''<math>k</math>''.<ref name=":5">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3w9eR3u8GN4C&q=Combinatorics+on+words.+Christoffel+words+and+repetitions+in+words+2009|title=Combinatorics on Words: Christoffel Words and Repetitions in Words|publisher=American Mathematical Soc.|isbn=978-0-8218-7325-0|pages=127|language=en}}</ref>

If pattern <math>p</math> is '''<math>k</math>'''-avoidable, then <math>p</math> is '''<math>g</math>'''-avoidable for all '''''<math>g\geq k</math>'''''.

Given a finite set of avoidable patterns <math>S=\{p_1,p_2,...,p_i \}</math>, there exists an infinite word <math>w\in\Sigma^\omega</math> such that <math>w</math> avoids all patterns of <math>S</math>.<ref name="Lothaire2001" /> Let <math>\mu(S)</math> denote the size of the minimal alphabet <math>\Sigma'</math>such that <math>\exist w' \in {\Sigma'}^\omega</math> avoiding all patterns of <math>S</math>.

=== Avoidability index ===
The avoidability index of a pattern ''<math>p</math>'' is the smallest ''<math>k</math>'' such that ''<math>p</math>'' is ''<math>k</math>''-avoidable, and ''<math>\infin</math>'' if ''<math>p</math>'' is unavoidable.<ref name="Lothaire2001" />

== Properties ==

*A pattern ''<math>q</math> ''is avoidable if ''<math>q</math> ''is an instance of an avoidable pattern ''<math>p</math>''.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last=Schmidt|first=Ursula|date=1987-08-01|title=Long unavoidable patterns|journal=Acta Informatica|language=en|volume=24|issue=4|pages=433–445|doi=10.1007/BF00292112|s2cid=7928450|issn=1432-0525}}</ref>
*Let avoidable pattern ''<math>p</math>'' be a factor of pattern ''<math>q</math>'', then ''<math>q</math>'' is also avoidable.<ref name=":1" />
*A pattern ''<math>q</math>'' is unavoidable if and only if ''<math>q</math>'' is a factor of some unavoidable pattern ''<math>p</math>''.
*Given an unavoidable pattern ''<math>p</math>'' and a symbol ''<math>a</math>'' not in ''<math>p</math>'', then ''<math>pap</math>'' is unavoidable.<ref name=":1" />
*Given an unavoidable pattern ''<math>p</math>'', then the [[Operations on languages|reversal]] ''<math>p^R</math>'' is unavoidable.
*Given an unavoidable pattern ''<math>p</math>'', there exists a symbol ''<math>a</math>'' such that ''<math>a</math>'' occurs exactly once in ''<math>p</math>''.<ref name=":1" />
*Let <math>n\in\Nu</math> represent the number of distinct symbols of pattern <math>p</math>. If <math>|p|\geq2^n</math>, then <math>p</math> is avoidable.<ref name=":1" />

== Zimin words ==
{{main|Sesquipower}}
Given alphabet <math>\Delta=\{x_1,x_2,...\}</math>, Zimin words (patterns) are defined recursively <math>Z_{n+1}=Z_nx_{n+1}Z_n</math> for <math>n\in\Zeta^+</math> and <math>Z_1=x_1</math>.

=== Unavoidability ===
All Zimin words are unavoidable.<ref name=":0" />

A word ''<math>w</math>'' is unavoidable if and only if it is a factor of a Zimin word.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Zimin|first=A. I.|title=Blocking Sets of Terms|date=1984|journal=Mathematics of the USSR-Sbornik|language=en|volume=47|issue=2|pages=353–364|doi=10.1070/SM1984v047n02ABEH002647|bibcode=1984SbMat..47..353Z|issn=0025-5734}}</ref>

Given a finite alphabet <math>\Sigma</math>, let <math>f(n,|\Sigma|)</math> represent the smallest <math>m\in\Zeta^+</math> such that <math>w</math> matches <math>Z_n</math> for all <math>w\in \Sigma^m</math>. We have following properties:<ref>{{cite arXiv | eprint=1409.3080 | last1=Cooper | first1=Joshua | last2=Rorabaugh | first2=Danny | title=Bounds on Zimin Word Avoidance | date=2014 | class=math.CO }}</ref>

*<math>f(1,q)=1</math>
*<math>f(2,q)=2q+1</math>
*<math>f(3,2)=29</math>
*<math>f(n,q)\leq{^{n-1}q}=\underbrace{q^{q^{\cdot^{\cdot^{q}}}}}_{n-1} </math>

<math>Z_n</math> is the longest unavoidable pattern constructed by alphabet <math>\Delta=\{x_1,x_2,...,x_n\}</math> since <math>|Z_n|=2^n -1</math>.

== Pattern reduction ==

=== Free letter ===
Given a pattern ''<math>p</math>'' over some alphabet <math>\Delta</math>, we say <math>x\in\Delta</math> is free for ''<math>p</math>'' if there exist subsets <math>A,B</math> of <math>\Delta</math> such that the following hold:

#<math>uv</math> is a factor of ''<math>p</math>'' and ''<math>u\in A</math>'' ↔  <math>uv</math> is a factor of ''<math>p</math>'' and ''<math>v\in B</math>''
#''<math>x\in A\backslash B\cup B\backslash A</math>''

For example, let ''<math>p=abcbab</math>'', then ''<math>b</math>'' is free for ''<math>p</math>'' since there exist ''<math>A=ac,B=b</math>'' satisfying the conditions above.

=== Reduce ===
A pattern ''<math>p\in \Delta^*</math>'' '''reduces''' to pattern ''<math>q</math>'' if there exists a symbol ''<math>x\in \Delta</math>'' such that ''<math>x</math>'' is free for ''<math>p</math>'', and ''<math>q</math>'' can be obtained by removing all occurrence of ''<math>x</math>'' from ''<math>p</math>''. Denote this relation by <math>p\stackrel{x}{\rightarrow}q</math>.

For example, let ''<math>p=abcbab</math>'', then ''<math>p</math>'' can reduce to ''<math>q=aca</math>'' since ''<math>b</math>'' is free for ''<math>p</math>''.

=== Locked ===
A word ''<math>w</math>'' is said to be locked if ''<math>w</math>'' has no free letter; hence ''<math>w</math>'' can not be reduced.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|last1=Baker|first1=Kirby A.|last2=McNulty|first2=George F.|last3=Taylor|first3=Walter|date=1989-12-18|title=Growth problems for avoidable words|journal=Theoretical Computer Science|language=en|volume=69|issue=3|pages=319–345|doi=10.1016/0304-3975(89)90071-6|issn=0304-3975|doi-access=free}}</ref>

=== Transitivity ===
Given patterns ''<math>p,q,r</math>'', if ''<math>p</math>'' reduces to ''<math>q</math>'' and ''<math>q</math>'' reduces to ''<math>r</math>'', then ''<math>p</math>'' reduces to ''<math>r</math>''. Denote this relation by <math>p\stackrel{*}{\rightarrow}r</math>.

=== Unavoidability ===
A pattern ''<math>p</math>'' is unavoidable if and only if ''<math>p</math>'' reduces to a word of length one; hence ''<math>\exist w</math>'' such that ''<math>|w|=1</math>'' and ''<math>p\stackrel{*}{\rightarrow}w</math>''.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Bean|first1=Dwight R.|last2=Ehrenfeucht|first2=Andrzej|last3=McNulty|first3=George F.|date=1979|title=Avoidable patterns in strings of symbols.|url=https://projecteuclid.org/euclid.pjm/1102783913|journal=Pacific Journal of Mathematics|language=en|volume=85|issue=2|pages=261–294|doi=10.2140/pjm.1979.85.261|issn=0030-8730|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name=":0" />

== Graph pattern avoidance==
Source:<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal|last=Grytczuk|first=Jarosław|date=2007-05-28|title=Pattern avoidance on graphs|journal=Discrete Mathematics|series=The Fourth Caracow Conference on Graph Theory|language=en|volume=307|issue=11|pages=1341–1346|doi=10.1016/j.disc.2005.11.071|issn=0012-365X|doi-access=free}}</ref>
=== Avoidance / Matching on a specific graph ===
Given a simple [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]] ''<math>G=(V,E)</math>'', a edge [[Graph coloring|coloring]] ''<math>c:E\rightarrow \Delta</math>'' matches pattern ''<math>p</math>'' if there exists a simple [[Path (graph theory)|path]] ''<math>P=[e_1,e_2,...,e_r]</math>'' in ''<math>G</math>'' such that the sequence ''<math>c(P)=[c(e_1),c(e_2),...,c(e_r)]</math>'' matches ''<math>p</math>''. Otherwise, ''<math>c</math>'' is said to avoid ''<math>p</math>'' or be ''<math>p</math>''-free.

Similarly, a vertex coloring ''<math>c:V\rightarrow \Delta</math>'' matches pattern ''<math>p</math>'' if there exists a simple [[Path (graph theory)|path]] ''<math>P=[c_1,c_2,...,c_r]</math>'' in ''<math>G</math>'' such that the sequence ''<math>c(P)</math>'' matches ''<math>p</math>''.

=== Pattern chromatic number ===
The pattern chromatic number <math>\pi_p(G)</math> is the minimal number of distinct colors needed for a ''<math>p</math>''-free vertex coloring ''<math>c</math>'' over the graph ''<math>G</math>''.

Let ''<math>\pi_p(n)=\max\{\pi_p(G):G\in G_n\}</math>'' where  ''<math>G_n</math>'' is the set of all simple graphs with a maximum [[Degree (graph theory)|degree]] no more than ''<math>n</math>''. 

Similarly, <math>\pi_p'(G)</math> and <math>\pi_p'(n)</math> are defined for edge colorings. 

=== Avoidability / Unavoidability on graphs ===
A pattern ''<math>p</math>'' is avoidable on graphs if ''<math>\pi_p(n)</math>'' is bounded by ''<math>c_p</math>'', where ''<math>c_p</math>'' only depends on ''<math>p</math>''. 

* Avoidance on words can be expressed as a specific case of avoidance on graphs; hence a pattern <math>p</math> is avoidable on any finite alphabet if and only if <math>\pi_p(P_n) \leq c_p</math> for all <math>n \in\Zeta ^+ </math>, where <math>P_n</math> is a graph of <math>n</math> vertices concatenated.

=== Probabilistic bound on ''{{pi}}{{sub|p}}(n)'' ===
There exists an absolute constant <math>c</math>, such that ''<math>\pi_p(n)\leq cn^{\frac{m(p)}{m(p)-1}}\leq cn^2</math>'' for all patterns ''<math>p</math>'' with ''<math>m(p)\geq2</math>''.<ref name=":4" />

Given a pattern <math>p</math>, let <math>n</math> represent the number of distinct symbols of <math>p</math>. If <math>|p|\geq2^n</math>, then <math>p</math> is avoidable on graphs.

=== Explicit colorings ===
Given a pattern <math>p</math> such that ''<math>count_p(x)</math>'' is even for all ''<math>x\in p</math>'', then <math>\pi_p'(K_2^k)\leq2^k-1</math> for all ''<math>k\geq 1</math>'', where ''<math>K_n</math>'' is the [[complete graph]] of <math>n</math> vertices.<ref name=":4" />

Given a pattern <math>p</math> such that ''<math>m(p)\geq2</math>'', and an arbitrary [[Tree (graph theory)|tree]] <math>T</math>, let <math>S</math> be the set of all avoidable subpatterns and their reflections of <math>p</math>. Then <math>\pi_p(T)\leq 3\mu(S)</math>.<ref name=":4" />

Given a pattern <math>p</math> such that ''<math>m(p)\geq2</math>'', and a [[Tree (graph theory)|tree]] <math>T</math> with degree ''<math>n\geq2</math>''. Let <math>S</math> be the set of all avoidable subpatterns and their reflections of <math>p</math>, then <math>\pi_p'(T)\leq 2(n-1)\mu(S)</math>.<ref name=":4" />

== Examples ==

* The [[Thue–Morse sequence]] is cube-free and overlap-free; hence it avoids the patterns ''<math>xxx</math>'' and ''<math>xyxyx</math>''.<ref name=":5" />
*A [[square-free word]] is one avoiding the pattern ''<math>xx</math>''. The word over the alphabet <math>\{0,\pm1\}</math> obtained by taking the [[first difference]] of the Thue–Morse sequence is an example of an infinite square-free word.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3w9eR3u8GN4C&q=Combinatorics+on+words.+Christoffel+words+and+repetitions+in+words+2009|title=Combinatorics on Words: Christoffel Words and Repetitions in Words|publisher=American Mathematical Soc.|isbn=978-0-8218-7325-0|pages=97|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Fogg|first=N. Pytheas|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qBIsuwEACAAJ&q=Substitutions+in+dynamics,+arithmetics+and+combinatorics.|title=Substitutions in Dynamics, Arithmetics and Combinatorics|date=2002-09-23|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|isbn=978-3-540-44141-0|pages=104|language=en}}</ref>
* The patterns ''<math>x</math>'' and ''<math>xyx</math>'' are unavoidable on any alphabet, since they are factors of the Zimin words.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Allouche|first1=Jean-Paul|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2ZsSUStt96sC&dq=Automatic+Sequences%3A+Theory%2C+Applications%2C+Generalizations&pg=PR13|title=Automatic Sequences: Theory, Applications, Generalizations|last2=Shallit|first2=Jeffrey|last3=Shallit|first3=Professor Jeffrey|date=2003-07-21|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0-521-82332-6|pages=24|language=en}}</ref><ref name="Lothaire2001" />
* The power patterns ''<math>x^n</math>'' for ''<math>n\geq 3 </math>'' are 2-avoidable.<ref name="Lothaire2001" />
*All binary patterns can be divided into three categories:<ref name="Lothaire2001">{{cite book|last1=Lothaire|first1=M.|url=https://archive.org/details/algebraiccombina0000loth|url-access=registration|title=Algebraic Combinatorics on Words|publisher=Cambridge University Press|year=2002|isbn=9780521812207}}</ref>
**<math>\varepsilon,x,xyx</math> are unavoidable.
**<math>xx,xxy,xyy,xxyx,xxyy,xyxx,xyxy,xyyx,xxyxx,xxyxy,xyxyy</math> have avoidability index of 3.
**others have avoidability index of 2.
*<math>abwbaxbcyaczca</math> has avoidability index of 4, as well as other locked words.<ref name=":3" />
*<math>abvacwbaxbcycdazdcd</math> has avoidability index of 5.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Clark|first=Ronald J.|date=2006-04-01|title=The existence of a pattern which is 5-avoidable but 4-unavoidable|journal=International Journal of Algebra and Computation|volume=16|issue=2|pages=351–367|doi=10.1142/S0218196706002950|issn=0218-1967}}</ref>
*The repetitive threshold <math>RT(n)</math> is the [[Infimum and supremum|infimum]] of exponents <math>k</math> such that <math>x^k</math> is avoidable on an alphabet of size <math>n</math>. Also see [[Dejean's theorem]].

== Open problems ==

*Is there an avoidable pattern <math>p</math> such that the avoidability index of <math>p</math> is 6?
*Given an arbitrarily pattern <math>p</math>, is there an algorithm to determine the avoidability index of <math>p</math>?<ref name="Lothaire2001" />
